comments.author: Alexander Terp
comments.body:
Measured, after the fact: the full ./dev took 43.8 minutes with the orphaned loops alive for part of the run, and 27.1 minutes on the next run with them dead - about a third of the gate, spent on nothing.

Neither number is a clean baseline. The first run spans both conditions, since the loops were killed partway through it, and the second still had another worktree compiling throughout. The uncontended cost is lower than 27 minutes and nobody has measured it.

Worth recording because it sizes the problem: the symptom was never an error, only a gate that took long enough to seem plausible. Half an hour is not obviously wrong for a run that builds two toolchains, which is exactly why seventy-four minutes of a machine being eaten went unnoticed - and why the integrator explained it with a wrong theory (parallel agents) and wrote that down as fact.

comments.author: Alexander Terp
comments.body:
Both halves landed. Every `./dev` run opens with a line like

    machine: 10 cores (6 performance), load 4.90 4.59 3.90

on the full gate and on narrowed flags alike, and turns yellow with a clause when the fast cores are already committed. `./dev --doctor` names what is on the machine.

**The census this card's sibling asked for works, and it found the same thing again.** Running it here, twenty-two herdr processes: two were clients with no API socket at all, four were bound to sockets whose paths have since been deleted and are unreachable by anything, and of the sixteen still answering, exactly one - pid 11093, `~/.config/herdr/herdr.sock`, two panes in `~/src` - held anybody's work. Everything else was a smoke fixture, a test-harness daemon under `/tmp/muster-test/`, or a scratch directory. It was neither the oldest nor the youngest, so the doctor prints what each socket holds rather than sorting by age.

`lsof -a -p <pid> -U`, with the `-a`, as a_28YghIUw2's last comment corrects. The API socket turns out to be listed directly in that output beside `herdr-client.sock`, so the path is read rather than derived - one less thing to get wrong. Dialling is `HERDR_SOCKET_PATH=<path> herdr pane list`, and only when the pinned herdr is already downloaded.

**The load half, on this card's own framing.** Nothing here is evidence that stray daemons are why a gate is slow - a_28YghIUw2 measured twenty of them at 0.1% CPU together, and this run agrees. The doctor's third section, the busiest processes, is what would actually have caught the eight orphaned busy loops, and it is there for that reason. Load says the machine is busy; the process list says what is eating it; the daemon census is about knowing which process holds work before ending it.

creator: Alexander Terp
description:
On 2026-08-17 an agent investigating a_29eAVr11v needed a loaded machine to reproduce a wedge, so it made one:

```sh
for c in $(seq 1 8); do (while :; do :; done) & done
BURNERS=$(jobs -p)
for r in $(seq 1 8); do ... catch-hang.sh ... done
kill $BURNERS
```

The rounds finished, the shell that owned the jobs exited, and the `kill` never ran. Eight busy loops were orphaned to init and kept spinning at about 89% of a core each for seventy-four minutes - roughly seven of this machine's ten cores, continuously, while three agents and an integrator ran `./dev` against what was left.

Nothing said so. Not the shell that leaked them, not the gate they were taxing, not the agent that made them. The only symptom was that `./dev` took half an hour, and half an hour is not obviously wrong for a run that builds two toolchains - so the integrator attributed it to parallel agents and wrote that down as a fact about running agents in parallel. Load average was 22.34 against ten cores at the time, and 14.05 within seconds of the loops being killed.

The same family has bitten before from the other direction: a_28YghIUw2 records eight herdr processes on this machine, seven of them scratch daemons left by agent sessions, and no way to tell which held live work.

Two halves, separable, and the second is the one worth having:

- **Cleanup.** A rig that spawns background work should take it down when it dies rather than on the happy path - `trap` in a shell, a guard object in a test. That is a convention rather than a change, and conventions do not reach the ad-hoc one-liner an agent writes at the moment it needs one, which is exactly where this came from.
- **Detection.** Nothing in this repo reads what the machine is doing before judging it. `./dev` could sample load at the start and say what it found, which would have turned seventy-four invisible minutes into one line at the top of every run. Cheap, and it points somewhere.

Worth deciding rather than defaulting:

- **Warn, record, or refuse.** Refusing on a busy machine blocks legitimate work on a laptop that is also doing something else. Recording is honest and ignorable. Warning is the middle, and the middle is where warnings get tuned out - unless the number is in every run's header rather than raised only when it is bad.
- **What the number is.** Load average needs a core count beside it to mean anything, and it is per-OS - so this is the shell's answer to hand over rather than the core's, the same as the log path and the screens.
- **Whether the perf tier is different.** a_28UsunMWa already wants this and has the strongest claim: it judges nanoseconds against a checked-in baseline, so a loaded machine does not slow it down, it makes it lie. Refusing to judge is defensible there and nowhere else.
- **Whether stray processes deserve their own check.** Load says the machine is busy, not what is eating it. A `./dev --doctor` that names what this repo's own tooling has left running - herdr daemons, devenv containers, orphaned harnesses - is the version that answers the next question too, and a_28YghIUw2 wants half of it already.
title: 🔥 A machine being eaten looks exactly like a slow gate
